title: What If an Island on the Map Didn't Exist? In 2012 a Ship Sailed Through It

scenes.text: What if an island on the map simply wasn't there? In 2012, scientists sailed straight through one.
Sandy Island sat in the Coral Sea on charts, in scientific databases, even on Google Earth: 25 kilometres long, five wide.
It was first reported in 1876 by a whaling ship, the Velocity. Then it was copied from map to map for more than a century.
In 2012 an Australian research ship, the Southern Surveyor, noticed its sea charts didn't match the maps. So the scientists went to look.
Where the island should have been, they found open ocean, 1,400 metres deep.
The best guess is that the whalers saw a giant raft of floating pumice from an undersea volcano. A rock that floats kept an island on the map for 136 years.

description:
What if an island that appeared on maps for over a century had never existed? Sandy Island, in the eastern Coral Sea, was shown as a 25 by 5 kilometre strip of land on charts, in the World Vector Shoreline Database and on Google Earth.
It was first reported by the whaling ship Velocity in 1876. In 2012 scientists aboard the Australian research vessel Southern Surveyor sailed to the spot and found water about 1,400 metres deep. The leading explanation is that the whalers saw a large raft of floating pumice from a volcanic eruption.
